items.title: Water is densest at 4 degrees Celsius, not zero
items.claim: Cool any substance and it gets denser as it approaches freezing — except water. Water reaches maximum density at 4 degrees Celsius and then becomes LESS dense as it cools further to 0 degrees Celsius.
items.prompt: Why does ice float on liquid water?

options.text: Trapped air bubbles make ice less dense than liquid water
Hydrogen bonds force water molecules into an open hexagonal lattice on freezing, so solid water occupies about 9 percent more volume than liquid water
Ice is colder, and colder things float
Surface tension on the underside of ice holds it up

items.reveal_title: Hydrogen bonding wins over packing efficiency
items.reveal:
In liquid water, hydrogen bonds break and re-form constantly, and molecules can crowd together. When water freezes, every molecule locks into a tetrahedral arrangement where each oxygen hydrogen-bonds to exactly four neighbours. That structure is open and roomy — about 9 percent more volume than the liquid.

This is why ponds freeze top-down rather than bottom-up. Fish survive winter because the densest water (4 degrees Celsius) sinks and the ice layer insulates everything below. If water behaved normally, lakes would freeze solid and life as we know it could not exist.
items.why: Students assume cooling always increases density. The hydrogen bond's geometry, not the temperature, controls the packing.

items.title: Benzene has no double bonds — and no single bonds
items.claim: Draw benzene the textbook way and you get alternating single and double bonds. But every carbon-carbon bond in benzene is exactly the same length: 139 picometres.
items.prompt: If a normal C-C single bond is 154 pm and a C=C double bond is 134 pm, what is going on?

options.text: The bonds flip back and forth so fast we measure the average
The six pi electrons are delocalised into a ring above and below the plane of the carbons — every bond has bond order 1.5
Benzene actually has three single and three double bonds; the textbook value of 139 pm is wrong
Each carbon has one and a half hydrogens on average

items.reveal_title: Aromaticity — delocalisation as a real, measurable thing
items.reveal:
Each carbon in benzene is sp2 hybridised. It contributes one electron to a p-orbital perpendicular to the ring. These six p-orbitals overlap sideways all the way around, forming two continuous doughnut-shaped pi clouds — one above the ring, one below.

The Kekulé structure with alternating bonds is not 'wrong' — it is one of two resonance structures. But the molecule is the average, with all bonds equivalent. Aromaticity also explains why benzene resists addition reactions that would break the ring's stability.
items.why: The line-and-double-line notation is a 19th century compromise. Quantum mechanics shows the real picture: delocalised electrons in a ring.

items.title: Carbon monoxide's dipole points the wrong way
items.claim: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon (3.44 versus 2.55). You would expect carbon monoxide to have a dipole with the negative end on oxygen. In fact the negative end sits on carbon.
items.prompt: Why does CO's dipole point from O (positive) to C (negative)?

options.text: Electronegativity values are wrong for small molecules
Oxygen donates a lone pair into a bonding orbital concentrated on carbon — the dative pi back-bonding cancels and reverses the simple electronegativity dipole
Carbon monoxide has no dipole at all
The molecule rotates so fast the dipole averages to zero

items.reveal_title: Molecular orbital theory beats Pauling's electronegativity table
items.reveal:
Drawing CO with a triple bond shows it as :C≡O: with a lone pair on each atom. But molecular orbital calculations and experiment agree: the highest occupied molecular orbital is the sigma orbital pointing AWAY from oxygen on the carbon side, giving carbon partial negative character.

This is exactly why CO is such a good ligand for transition metals — it bonds to metals through the carbon, donating that lone pair while accepting back-donation into empty pi-star orbitals. The whole of transition-metal carbonyl chemistry depends on it.
items.why: Electronegativity gives a crude bond-polarity estimate. For molecules with multiple bonds and lone pairs, the orbital picture matters more.
